notes: Adult teeth wait under the baby ones

blocks.prompt: Why Your Tooth Wiggles
blocks.text: You have twenty baby teeth. Each one has a job. The flat teeth at the front bite into an apple. The wide teeth at the back grind the apple up so you can swallow it. Under your baby teeth, bigger teeth are waiting in your jaw. When a big tooth is ready, it starts to push up. The root of the baby tooth melts away to make room. That is why the tooth wiggles. Soon it falls out, and the new tooth takes its place. When you are grown up you will have up to thirty-two teeth. Those ones have to last. So brush them well.

notes: The white part is called enamel

blocks.prompt: The Hardest Thing Your Body Makes
blocks.text: Bite down and feel how solid that is. The shiny white outside of your tooth is called enamel, and it is the hardest thing your body makes. It is harder than your bones. Enamel is almost all mineral, packed into tiny crystals lined up like bricks in a wall. That wall lets you crunch ice and chew tough crusts for eighty years without wearing through. But enamel has one big problem. It is not alive. Your bones are full of living cells, so a broken bone can slowly knit itself back together and be as good as new. Enamel has no living cells at all. Once a piece of it is gone, it is gone for good. Your tooth is the only part of you that cannot heal itself. That is why brushing matters so much. Tiny living things called bacteria sit on your teeth. They eat the sugar you eat, and then they make acid. The acid dissolves the mineral in your enamel a little at a time, until a hole opens up. We call that hole a cavity. A dentist can fill the hole, but your body will never grow the enamel back.

notes: Dentin is full of microscopic tubes

blocks.prompt: Layers, and Why Cold Hurts
blocks.text: A tooth looks like a solid white pebble. It is not. It is built in layers, and every layer has a different job. The outside layer is enamel, almost pure mineral and the hardest material your body produces, harder than any bone. Enamel takes the beating. Underneath it sits dentin, softer and slightly yellow. Dentin is not solid either. It is drilled through with millions of microscopic tubes, far too small to see, running from the outside of the tooth toward the middle. In the middle is the pulp, a soft chamber packed with blood vessels and nerves. Below the gum, the root is coated in a layer called cementum and held in its socket by a sling of stretchy fibers, so your tooth can flex a whisker when you bite. Now you can explain something you have felt. When you drink something ice cold and a tooth stings, the cold is not touching the nerve. It is pushing on the fluid inside those tiny dentin tubes. The fluid shifts, the nerve in the pulp feels it move, and it reports pain. If enamel wears thin, more tubes are open to the outside, and the sting gets sharper. People call teeth bones, but they are not. Bone is living tissue that takes itself apart and rebuilds itself for your whole life. Enamel has no cells and rebuilds nothing. That is also why you get exactly two sets: twenty baby teeth, then up to thirty-two adult ones. A shark grows a fresh row every few weeks and never runs out. You get one spare set, and after that you are on your own.

notes: Plaque is a living film of bacteria

blocks.prompt: The Slow War in Your Mouth
blocks.text: Your mouth is never still. Even now, a thin living film is forming on your teeth. It is called plaque, and it is not leftover food. It is a city of bacteria, millions of them, gluing themselves to your enamel in layers. Most of those bacteria are harmless. A few are not, and the worst of them has a name: Streptococcus mutans. It eats what you eat. Feed it sugar and it produces acid within minutes. That acid does something very specific. It pulls calcium and phosphate out of the enamel crystals underneath it. Scientists call this demineralization. Nothing hurts. Nothing looks different. The enamel is simply losing material from just below its surface. Then your body pushes back. Saliva floods in, rinses the sugar away, buffers the acid, and carries dissolved calcium and phosphate of its own. Over the next hour or two it hands those minerals back and repairs the damaged crystals. That is remineralization, and it happens every day of your life. A tooth is not a stone sitting quietly in your jaw. It is a battlefield, losing mineral and regaining it, over and over. A cavity is what happens when the losses beat the gains for long enough. The weakened surface finally collapses inward, and once there is a real hole, the war is over. Enamel has no living cells, so it cannot grow a patch across a gap. Only a dentist can close it. This explains a rule that sounds strange until you know the chemistry. Sipping one soda slowly across a whole afternoon does more damage than drinking the same can in five minutes. The amount of sugar is not what matters most. What matters is the number of hours your enamel spends sitting in acid, never getting the quiet time it needs to rebuild. Fluoride is the other half of the story. When fluoride is present while a tooth is remineralizing, it gets built into the crystal in place of part of the original recipe. The rebuilt enamel is a slightly different mineral, and it takes a stronger acid to dissolve it. Fluoride does not sit on your teeth like paint. It joins them, and it makes the repair tougher than the original ever was.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ameloblasts build it, then die before the tooth erupts
Enamel forms in daily layers, like tree rings
The neonatal line marks the moment of birth
Diphyodont: humans get exactly two sets
An elephant gets six sets of molars, then starves

blocks.prompt: The Tissue That Cannot Forget
blocks.text: Every other part of you is in the business of replacing itself. Your skin sheds and rebuilds. Your bones are quietly dismantled and reconstructed by cells that work your entire life, which is why a snapped arm can knit back into a working arm. Your blood is renewed within months. Enamel does none of this. Enamel is laid down once, finished, and abandoned. That sounds like a design failure, and in one sense it is. Enamel is roughly ninety-six percent mineral, packed into long crystal rods bundled tightly together, and that extreme mineral content is exactly what makes it the hardest substance your body produces. Living tissue cannot be that hard. Cells need water, space, and supply lines, and enamel has almost none of any of them. The cells that build it, called ameloblasts, finish their work before the tooth ever erupts into your mouth, and then they die. Every adult tooth you own arrived complete and has been wearing down ever since. It is the only part of you that cannot heal itself. But the same property that makes enamel unable to repair makes it something no other tissue can be. Bone erases its own history as it rebuilds. Enamel cannot erase anything, because it cannot rebuild anything. So it keeps everything. Put a tooth under a microscope and you find lines, stacked like the rings of a tree. Enamel forms in daily increments, and each day leaves a faint stripe in the crystal. Count the stripes and you can count the days that tooth spent forming. One line is heavier and darker than the rest, and every human being who has ever lived carries it in their baby teeth. Anatomists call it the neonatal line. It marks the moment of birth. The shock of leaving the womb interrupts enamel formation briefly, and the interruption is written into the mineral permanently. Your teeth carry a physical mark of the day you were born. The record runs deeper than dates. The minerals in enamel are drawn from what a child eats and drinks while the tooth is forming, and the chemical signature of drinking water differs from region to region. Because enamel never remodels, that signature is locked in for life, and it survives long after the rest of a body is gone. This is why archaeologists prize teeth above almost anything else they dig up. From a single medieval tooth, researchers can estimate where its owner grew up, roughly when they stopped nursing, and whether their childhood included seasons of hunger, because starvation interrupts enamel formation and leaves its own visible lines. So the trade is clear. You could have teeth that heal, but they would be soft, and soft teeth cannot process a lifetime of grain and gristle and ice. Evolution chose hardness and accepted the cost. Humans are diphyodont, meaning we get exactly two sets and no more: twenty as children, up to thirty-two as adults. Other animals struck different bargains. Sharks run a conveyor belt of replacement teeth and shed thousands in a lifetime. An elephant is issued six sets of grinding molars that slide forward one after another as each wears out, and when the last set is gone, the animal starves, no matter how healthy the rest of it is. Your enamel will not be reissued either. It is the hardest thing you will ever grow, the only thing you own that remembers your birth, and the one part of you that a toothbrush protects better than your own body ever can.
